subject: Automotive & EVs
title: LFP: The Budget Champion
description: A micro-lesson that makes LFP: The Budget Champion usable.

hook.text: Lithium iron phosphate batteries use no cobalt or nickel—just iron, the cheapest metal on Earth.

buildup.text: LFP cells are safer, longer-lasting, and far cheaper than NMC, but they store less energy per kilogram.

discovery.text: BYD's Blade Battery uses LFP in a cell-to-pack design that closes the range gap with NMC.

twist.text: Tesla switched its standard-range models to LFP, signaling that cheaper batteries had finally become good enough.

climax.text: LFP now powers over half of all EVs sold in China and is rapidly gaining share worldwide.

punchline.text: Iron and phosphate proved that cheap can also be excellent.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of LFP batteries over NMC?

details.summary: Lithium iron phosphate batteries use iron instead of cobalt or nickel, offering lower cost, longer cycle life, and greater thermal stability at the expense of slightly lower energy density.
details.whyItMatters: LFP has become the chemistry of choice for affordable EVs and energy storage. Its safety advantages and low cost are rapidly expanding the market for electric vehicles at mainstream price points.
takeaways: LFP avoids expensive and ethically problematic cobalt
It offers over 3,000 charge cycles with minimal degradation
Tesla and BYD use LFP in their most affordable models

faq.question: Why does LFP have lower energy density than NMC batteries?
faq.answer: Iron has a lower voltage potential than nickel or cobalt, which reduces the energy each cell can store. The trade-off is much better thermal stability, longer life, and significantly lower material cost.

faq.question: Is LFP safe enough to not need active cooling?
faq.answer: LFP is far more thermally stable than NMC, and some lower-power applications skip active cooling. However, EVs typically still include thermal management to optimize performance and lifespan.
